title: Expository vs. Topical Preaching: Which Should You Preach?
subtitle: An honest comparison of expository and topical preaching, the strengths and dangers of each, and how to decide which approach serves your congregation and the text.

sections.title: The Tribal Lines Are Lying to You
sections.body:
Ask the question in most rooms and you have already started a fight. You do not need to.

One camp treats expository preaching as the only faithful kind and topical preaching as a worldly compromise for men who will not do the work. The other camp treats expository preaching as a dull march through verses for an audience nobody can find anymore. Both have made an idol of a method. The real question is not which label you wear. It is whether the point of your sermon is the point of God's Word, and whether the people in front of you can receive it. You can fail at that with either approach. You can succeed at it with either approach.

So put down the tribe. The honest question is simpler and harder. What does faithful preaching require, and which approach serves it this week, with this text, for these people.

sections.title: What Exposition Protects
sections.body:
Expository preaching, working through a book paragraph by paragraph, has one great strength that nothing else matches. It takes the agenda out of your hands.

When the text sets the menu, you preach things you would never have chosen. You arrive at the verse on money the week you wanted to talk about grace, at judgment when your instinct was comfort, at the very sin your congregation is committing because the next paragraph happens to name it. You cannot ride your three favorite themes for thirty years, because the book will not let you. Over time your people get the whole counsel of God, the bitter and the sweet, and they learn that the authority is in the Bible and not in your preferences. They also learn how to read for themselves, because they have watched you do it five hundred times.

The danger is real too. Exposition can become a running commentary with no spine, a verse-by-verse crawl that never gathers into a single piercing point. Done lazily it informs the head and never lands on the heart. Exposition is not an excuse to avoid the hard work of finding the one thing this passage demands today.

sections.title: What Topical Preaching Reaches
sections.body:
Topical preaching starts with a subject and gathers the Bible's teaching on it. Done with integrity, it does something exposition cannot.

Some questions do not live in a single passage. What does the whole Bible say about suffering. About money. About anxiety, marriage, the will of God. A grieving congregation, a community in crisis, a cultural moment that demands an answer, these sometimes call for a sermon that draws the threads together from across Scripture. Topical preaching can also be the front door for the outsider, the seeker who came with a question and would never have walked in for week eleven of Leviticus. Jesus and the apostles both preached this way when the moment required it.

The danger is the obvious one. Topical preaching can become a man with a point in search of verses, the Bible reduced to evidence in a case he already decided in the car. It tempts you to your hobby horses and your safe themes. The discipline that saves it is brutal honesty. Are you letting Scripture shape the topic, or are you using Scripture to decorate your own conclusions.

sections.title: Let the Sheep and the Text Decide
sections.body:
The choice is not about your taste. It is about what your people need and what the text in front of you is.

A young congregation that has never been fed needs the bones of a book, the slow steady diet that exposition gives. A church reeling from a tragedy may need a topical sermon on suffering more than the next chapter of Acts. A season of confusion about a doctrine may call for a topical series that builds the case. Most healthy preaching ministries do both across a year, anchored in long expository runs and punctuated by topical series when the moment demands it. The book gives the backbone. The topic meets the need the backbone did not happen to address this month.

The one thing you cannot do is choose the approach that lets you avoid the work. Both done well are hard. Both done lazily are useless. The method is not your master. Faithfulness is.

sections.title: The Question Under the Question
sections.body:
Strip away the labels and one test remains for any sermon you preach.

Did the people meet God in his Word, or did they meet you in your opinions. That is the whole of it. An expository sermon can fail that test, a long performance of study that left the text unopened and the heart untouched. A topical sermon can pass it, a clear and burning word from the whole of Scripture that left people on their knees. The form is not the faithfulness. The form is the vehicle. The faithfulness is whether the living God spoke through his own Word to the people he loves.

So stop asking which camp is right. Ask the only question that matters on Sunday. Did they leave having heard from God. If they did, you preached. If they did not, no method will save you.
